entries.prompt: Part 1 — The writer in trouble
entries.answer: John Hallock is a writer who earns his living by writing ghost stories for Jenkin's magazine — though he dislikes the task and finds it hard to invent plots. His publisher, Jenkins, is pressing him for a new story, and John sits at his desk, unable to think of anything. Suddenly a ghost materialises before him — an owl-eyed, unattractive female spirit. She is part of "The Writer's Inspiration Bureau": ghosts like her have been supplying writers with their plots, sitting on their shoulders and whispering ideas.

entries.prompt: Part 2 — The ghost on strike
entries.answer: The ghost, Helen, tells John that the ghosts are on strike. Too many people have taken to using Ouija boards, summoning spirits for silly questions, and the ghosts are exhausted and resent being treated as entertainers. Until people give up their Ouija boards, the Inspiration Bureau will supply no more plots. Helen asks John to use his influence to stop his friends from using Ouija boards. John is horrified, therefore, when his wife Lavinia comes home and proudly announces that she has bought an Ouija board.

entries.prompt: Part 3 — The Ouija board party
entries.answer: Lavinia, who loves new fashions and fads, invites her friends to a Ouija board party at their house. John is forced to take part, dreading what the ghost had warned him about. During the séance the board spells out strange words — and to John's horror, the name "Helen" appears, along with words that make him seem a traitor to his wife. Lavinia, already suspicious, now believes her husband is having an affair with a woman named Helen. She decides to leave him.

entries.prompt: Part 4 — The misunderstanding cleared
entries.answer: As Lavinia packs to leave, Helen appears to her. The ghost explains who she really is — the spirit who had been helping John with his stories — and tells her that the name on the Ouija board was hers, not the name of any earthly rival. Lavinia's misunderstanding is cleared, and she and John are reconciled. Gladolia, the terrified maid, declares the Ouija board a "hoodoo" and refuses to stay. The board is thrown into the fire, and John, delighted at the turn of events, at last has the plot for his new ghost story.

entries.prompt: Superstition and the craze for the supernatural
entries.answer: The story satirises the fashion for spiritualism and Ouija boards. Lavinia buys a board because it is the latest trend, her friends gather for séances as a party game, and the ghosts themselves go on strike because they are tired of being summoned for trivial questions. The theme mocks blind credulity: people who play with forces they do not understand — and the Ouija board, meant to be harmless fun, nearly destroys John's marriage through a mere misunderstanding.

entries.prompt: Trust and misunderstanding in marriage
entries.answer: The story turns on a domestic misunderstanding. Lavinia's suspicion that John is involved with a woman named Helen is built entirely on the words spelled out by the Ouija board — a few letters that are, in truth, the name of a ghost. Because she trusts the board more than her husband, the misunderstanding grows until she packs to leave. The theme teaches the value of trust and communication: had Lavinia asked John directly, the whole storm could have been avoided. Superstition, the story suggests, feeds on mistrust.

entries.prompt: The writer's struggle for inspiration
entries.answer: John Hallock is a reluctant writer whose inspiration literally comes from ghosts — the members of the "Writer's Inspiration Bureau" who whisper plots into writers' ears. When the ghosts go on strike, John is helpless before his blank page. The theme satirises the writing life: inspiration is mysterious, unreliable, and often felt to come from outside oneself. The story's joke is that John's supernatural helpers are as real to him as his publisher's demands — and that his best story arrives precisely when he stops trying to force it.

entries.prompt: John Hallock
entries.answer: John Hallock is the narrator, a writer of ghost stories for Jenkin's magazine, though he has little love for the genre and struggles for plots. He is a mild, hen-pecked husband, afraid of his fashionable wife, and dependent for his inspiration on the ghost Helen, who supplies him with plots. He is honest and good-natured — caught between his publisher's demands, his wife's suspicions and the demands of the striking ghosts. His great moment comes when he simply tells Lavinia the truth, and the misunderstanding dissolves.

entries.prompt: Lavinia
entries.answer: Lavinia is John's wife — pretty, fashionable and given to the latest fads, with an alarming tendency to spend money on new trends. It is she who buys the Ouija board and organises the séance party, and it is her ready suspicion, fed by the board's messages, that nearly breaks the marriage. Yet she is not unkind: her jealousy springs from love, and once Helen explains the truth, she is reconciled at once, and the board goes into the fire. She represents the human weakness for superstition and the strength of a loving heart that can forgive.

entries.prompt: Helen, the ghost
entries.answer: Helen is an owl-eyed, unattractive ghost, a member of "The Writer's Inspiration Bureau" who supplies plots to writers. She appears to John when he is stuck, materialising in parts — a hand, then a face — like a moving-picture cartoon. She is sharp-tongued and fed up: the ghosts have gone on strike because people abuse Ouija boards. Yet she is friendly to John and finally saves his marriage by revealing herself to Lavinia. She is a comic figure — a ghost who is more like a harassed office worker than a spirit of terror.

entries.prompt: Gladolia
entries.answer: Gladolia is the Hallocks' maid, a minor but memorable figure. She is terrified of the Ouija board and its works, declaring it a "hoodoo" and refusing to stay in the house while it is used. Her simple, fearful faith serves as comic contrast to the fashionable credulity of Lavinia and her friends — and as the story's sly comment: the least educated person in the tale is the one who most sensibly refuses to play with the supernatural.

entries.prompt: Trust your loved ones before hearsay
entries.answer: The story teaches the value of trust in relationships. Lavinia believes the letters on a Ouija board over the word of her own husband, and her misplaced suspicion nearly ends the marriage. The lesson: doubt based on superstition or gossip is destructive; love is built on faith in one another. Ask, speak and listen — the truth, as the story shows, is usually far simpler and more innocent than suspicion imagines.

entries.prompt: Do not dabble in what you do not understand
entries.answer: The story cautions against playing with forces one does not control. The Ouija board is taken up as a party amusement, yet it disrupts a household, terrifies the maid, and nearly ruins a marriage — all on the strength of letters that mean nothing. The value lesson: superstition and credulity make us fools; reason, patience and honest conversation solve what magic cannot. The ghosts, after all, were on strike against being summoned by the credulous.

entries.prompt: What did John Hallock write for a living?
entries.answer: He wrote ghost stories for Jenkin's magazine, though he did not enjoy writing them and struggled for plots.

entries.prompt: Why were the ghosts on strike?
entries.answer: Because too many people were using Ouija boards, summoning spirits for trivial questions, and the ghosts were exhausted and fed up.

entries.prompt: How did Helen appear to John?
entries.answer: She materialised in parts — first a hand, then other body parts — like a moving-picture cartoon, and was owl-eyed and unattractive.

entries.prompt: What was "The Writer's Inspiration Bureau"?
entries.answer: The ghosts' organisation that supplied writers with their plots, sitting on their shoulders and whispering ideas.

entries.prompt: Who bought the Ouija board?
entries.answer: Lavinia, John's wife, who loved new fashions and fads, bought it and organised a séance party with her friends.

entries.prompt: What did the Ouija board spell out at the party?
entries.answer: The name "Helen" and words that made John seem a traitor, leading Lavinia to suspect him of an affair.

entries.prompt: Why did Lavinia decide to leave John?
entries.answer: She believed the board's messages meant her husband was unfaithful to her with a woman named Helen.

entries.prompt: How was the misunderstanding cleared?
entries.answer: Helen the ghost appeared to Lavinia and explained that she was the spirit who helped John with his stories, not an earthly rival.

entries.prompt: What did Gladolia call the Ouija board?
entries.answer: A "hoodoo" — she was terrified of it and refused to stay in the house while it was used.

entries.prompt: How did the story end?
entries.answer: Lavinia and John were reconciled, the Ouija board was thrown into the fire, and John at last had the plot for his new ghost story.

entries.prompt: Describe John Hallock's encounter with the ghost Helen.
entries.answer: John was stuck for a plot, as usual, when the ghost appeared in his study. She took shape slowly and comically — a hand materialising first, then other parts, like the frames of a moving-picture cartoon — until a whole woman stood before him: owl-eyed and far from beautiful, the last thing one would expect of a spirit. She announced that she was part of "The Writer's Inspiration Bureau", the organisation through which ghosts supplied writers with their plots by sitting on their shoulders and whispering ideas. Then she made her astonishing complaint: the ghosts were on strike. Modern people had taken up Ouija boards in droves, summoning spirits to answer silly questions, and the ghosts were sick of being treated as entertainers. Until the world gave up its Ouija boards, she warned, no more inspiration would flow. She asked John to discourage his friends from using the boards — a request that filled him with dread, for at that very moment his wife Lavinia was arriving home with a brand-new Ouija board she had bought.

entries.prompt: How did the Ouija board party nearly wreck John's marriage?
entries.answer: Lavinia, delighted with her fashionable new possession, invited her friends for a Ouija board séance. John, remembering the ghost's warning, was forced to join in, hoping nothing would go wrong. But as the friends sat round the board, it began to spell out words — and to John's horror, they were about him: the name "Helen" appeared, together with messages that branded him a traitor. To Lavinia, the meaning was plain: her husband was involved with a woman named Helen. In an instant the harmless party game turned into a domestic crisis. Lavinia, convinced of his guilt, packed her things and prepared to leave him. John, who could hardly explain that Helen was a ghost who supplied him with plots, stood helpless as the séance's idle letters did what no enemy could have done — they set his own wife against him, all on the strength of superstition.

entries.prompt: Describe the ending of the story. How is the misunderstanding resolved?
entries.answer: As Lavinia stood ready to leave, the ghost Helen appeared before her. In that moment the truth came out: Helen explained that she was the spirit of the "Writer's Inspiration Bureau" who had been helping John with his ghost stories, and that the name spelled out by the Ouija board was hers — a name from the world of spirits, not the name of any woman in John's life. Lavinia's jealousy, built on a few letters of a party game, collapsed before the absurd, wonderful truth. She and John were reconciled; the misunderstanding that superstition had built, honesty destroyed. Gladolia, the terrified maid, would have nothing more to do with the house's "hoodoo" and left her service. The Ouija board was thrown into the fire, and John — delighted to have his wife back, his ghost's strike and his troubles all resolved at once — realised that he had at last found the perfect plot for the ghost story Jenkins had been demanding. The story ends in laughter: the supernatural, treated seriously, had nearly ruined him; treated as the joke it is, it had saved his marriage and his career.

entries.prompt: Value question: What does the story teach us about superstition and trust?
entries.answer: The story teaches two related lessons. First, superstition is dangerous because it substitutes noise for sense: the Ouija board spells random letters, yet grown women build a domestic catastrophe on them, and a marriage nearly ends because of a ghost's name. The credulous pay for their credulity, while the sensible maid Gladolia — who simply calls the thing a "hoodoo" and keeps away — suffers nothing. Second, the story teaches the value of trust in marriage: Lavinia trusted a board more than her husband, and her suspicion did the work of any enemy. The remedy, as the ending shows, is honesty — the moment John tells the truth and Helen shows herself, every misunderstanding evaporates. The values the story presses on us are these: reason over superstition, trust over suspicion, and plain speech over the whispers of boards and mediums. Play with the supernatural, it warns, and you may find your own plot turned against you.

entries.prompt: Why can "A Shady Plot" be called a humorous ghost story?
entries.answer: Most ghost stories aim to frighten; this one aims to amuse, and it does so by turning every convention of the genre upside down. The ghost is not a horror but a harassed worker: Helen is owl-eyed, unattractive, sharp-tongued, and her great news is that the spirits have formed a union and gone on strike against overwork. The hero is not a brave investigator but a hen-pecked writer terrified of his wife. The great mystery is not a curse but a misread Ouija board, and the climax is not a haunting but a marital tiff. Even the ghost's appearance is comic — she materialises bit by bit, "like watching a moving-picture cartoon". And the resolution is pure farce: the ghost saves the marriage, the maid resigns over the "hoodoo", the board is burned, and the writer gets his plot. The humour lies in the contrast between the grand supernatural machinery — ghosts, séances, inspiration from beyond — and the homely domestic muddle it produces. Elsie Brown proves that the supernatural, treated lightly, is one of the best comic materials in literature.

entries.prompt: Scene 1 — Calpurnia's dream and the omens
entries.answer: On the morning of the Ides of March, Caesar's wife Calpurnia begs him not to go to the Senate. She has dreamt that a statue of Caesar, spouting blood, was bathed in the washing of a hundred Romans — a sign that his blood will be shed for the people. Calpurnia has also heard of terrible omens in the streets: a lioness whelping in the Capitol, the dead rising from their graves, men on fire who are not burned, and warriors fighting in the clouds. She pleads with Caesar to stay at home, and Caesar, moved by her fear, is half persuaded — until Decius Brutus arrives and reinterprets the dream as a good omen: the blood is not Caesar's but the people's love, and the senators have resolved to crown him today.

entries.prompt: Scene 2 — The Senate and the assassination
entries.answer: Caesar goes to the Capitol, where the conspirators wait. Metellus Cimber kneels, begging that the banishment of his brother Publius Cimber be reversed. Caesar refuses proudly, declaring that he is as constant as the northern star. The conspirators surround him, pretending to plead, and at a signal — Casca's "Speak, hands, for me!" — they stab him. Caesar sees his friend Brutus among the daggers and cries out, and falls dead at the foot of Pompey's statue, wrapped in his robe. The conspirators cry "Liberty! Freedom! Tyranny is dead!" and Brutus persuades them to bathe their hands in Caesar's blood as a symbol of their deed — but first he bids them not to harm Antony, and he and Cassius agree to face the people and justify the assassination.

entries.prompt: Scene 3 — Brutus's speech to the people
entries.answer: At the Forum, Brutus addresses the crowd. He declares that he loved Caesar, but that he loved Rome more: he asks the people if they would rather Caesar were alive and they all slaves, or Caesar dead and they all freemen. He explains that he killed Caesar for ambition — Caesar's ambition would have enslaved them — and he asks them to judge him as they judge him: "As I slew my best lover for the good of Rome, I have the same dagger for myself, when it shall please my country to need my death." The crowd is moved, and cries out that Brutus is an honourable man, that Caesar was a tyrant — and Brutus, satisfied, leaves the Forum, telling the people to stay and hear Caesar's funeral oration by Antony, who has his permission to speak.

entries.prompt: Scene 4 — Antony's funeral oration
entries.answer: Antony steps up with Caesar's body and turns the crowd. He opens with the famous address — "Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears" — and tells them that he has come to bury Caesar, not to praise him. In an irony that builds line by line, he calls the conspirators "honourable men" while showing that their reasons are false: Caesar enriched the people with the ransom money of captives, wept with the poor, and refused the crown three times at the Lupercal. He reads Caesar's will, in which Caesar leaves seventy-five drachmas to every Roman citizen and his walks, gardens and orchards to the people, to be enjoyed by all. The crowd, inflamed, rises against the conspirators, and Antony exults: "Now let it work."

entries.prompt: Scene 5 — The mob and the flight of the conspirators
entries.answer: The oration has done its work. The mob rushes through the streets crying "Caesar's better parts shall be crowned in Brutus!" and killing anyone who bears the name of a conspirator: the poet Cinna is torn to pieces merely for his name. Brutus and Cassius, warned that the city is lost, flee from Rome. Antony, with Octavius Caesar — the dead ruler's heir — and Lepidus, takes control of the city and sets about hunting the conspirators down. The play's excerpt ends with the civil struggle begun: the assassins are scattered, the people are with Antony, and the revenge for Caesar's murder is only beginning.

entries.prompt: Ambition and the fear of tyranny
entries.answer: The conspirators justify the assassination as a defence of liberty: they fear Caesar's ambition will make him king and enslave them. Brutus, the "noblest Roman of them all", kills his friend for the love of Rome, believing that one ambitious man must die that all may be free. The theme is double-edged: ambition is Caesar's supposed crime, but ambition — of Brutus, Cassius, Antony — drives the play. The fear of tyranny leads to murder, and murder leads to civil war. Shakespeare asks: when does a man's ambition threaten a state, and who is to judge — and at what cost?

entries.prompt: The power of rhetoric and persuasion
entries.answer: The excerpt is a study in the power of words. Brutus speaks first, and the crowd is his; Antony speaks second, and the crowd is lost to the conspirators. Antony's art lies in irony — "Brutus is an honourable man" — and in staging: he shows the bloody robe, he reads the will, he pauses to weep. Each device turns the people further. The theme is that public speech can move multitudes for good or ill, and that the crowd is fickle: it hailed Brutus, then tore Cinna apart. Rhetoric, Shakespeare shows, is the real battlefield — the daggers only begin the war.

entries.prompt: Fate, omens and free will
entries.answer: The scene is thick with portents: Calpurnia's dream of the statue spouting blood, the lioness whelping in the Capitol, the dead rising from their graves, the warring armies in the clouds. Caesar, who says "cowards die many times before their deaths", chooses to go to the Senate despite the warnings — or is led there by Decius's reinterpretation of the dream. The theme asks whether Caesar's fall was written in the stars or chosen by the men who feared him. The play's answer is characteristically Shakespearean: omens may warn, but men make the decisions — and pay the price.

entries.prompt: Friendship betrayed
entries.answer: The deepest wound in the scene is personal. Caesar dies not only at the hands of enemies but at the daggers of friends — above all of Brutus, whom he loved and trusted, and whose name is last on his lips. The friendship between Brutus and Caesar is the play's tragic hinge: Brutus joins the conspiracy out of conscience, not envy, and yet it is his betrayal that breaks Caesar's heart: "Et tu, Brute?" The theme is that political ideals, however noble, cannot cleanse a treacherous act; and that the noblest-seeming motive may be the most destructive.

entries.prompt: Julius Caesar
entries.answer: Caesar is the ruler of Rome, a great soldier and a proud man. He is superstitious yet self-confident: he mocks the soothsayer's warning, dismisses Calpurnia's dream until it is reinterpreted, and refuses Metellus Cimber's plea with the famous claim that he is as constant as the northern star. He is a man of appetite — the crowd speaks of his refusal of the crown three times, and his will leaves the people orchards and gardens — and of pride, which the conspirators use to lure him to the Capitol. His death at the foot of Pompey's statue, with Brutus's name on his lips, is the fall of a colossus.

entries.prompt: Brutus
entries.answer: Brutus is the noblest of the conspirators, loved by the people and loved by Caesar. He joins the conspiracy not for envy or gain but from principle — he fears what Caesar's ambition will do to Rome, and he is willing to sacrifice his friend for the republic. He is honourable and also naive: he refuses to harm Antony, allowing the funeral oration that destroys the conspiracy; he speaks honestly where Antony schemes. His speech moves the crowd, but he underestimates Antony's rhetoric. Brutus is the play's tragic figure of conscience: a good man whose deed, however reasoned, brings ruin.

entries.prompt: Mark Antony
entries.answer: Antony is Caesar's loyal friend and the conspirators' deadliest enemy. In the funeral oration he hides a master strategist inside a grieving mourner: weeping, showing the bloody robe, repeating that the conspirators are "honourable men" until the irony turns the crowd. He is shrewd, patient and ruthless — reading the will at exactly the right moment, waiting for the mob to do its work, and then seizing power with Octavius. Antony represents the theme of rhetoric: words, in his hands, are weapons more deadly than daggers, and he wins the city without striking a blow.

entries.prompt: Calpurnia
entries.answer: Calpurnia is Caesar's wife, the voice of foreboding in the scene. She has dreamt of his statue spouting blood, and she pleads with him with a wife's fear: "Do not go forth today." She has heard the omens of the streets — the lioness, the graves opening, the men in flames — and she reads them as warnings. Her fear is sound, and Caesar is almost persuaded; but Decius reinterprets the dream, and her warning is undone by rhetoric. Calpurnia embodies the play's theme of omens and fate: the truth was written in her dream, yet the tide of persuasion ran against it.

entries.prompt: Decius Brutus
entries.answer: Decius is the conspirator who ensures the plot succeeds. When Caesar, moved by Calpurnia, decides to stay home, Decius is sent for — and with a single stroke of flattery and reinterpretation he reverses the decision. He explains the dream anew: the blood in the statue's mouth is not Caesar's but Rome's love, the people washing themselves in it; and he adds that the Senate, having resolved to crown Caesar today, will think him afraid of his wife's dreams. The ambition in the dream's new meaning is exactly what Caesar wishes to believe. Decius shows how language can bend fate — and how Caesar's pride is his undoing.

entries.prompt: The common people of Rome
entries.answer: The crowd is itself a character in the scene. It gathers at the Forum, ready to be swayed; it applauds Brutus's reasoning; and it is turned in a single speech by Antony's art. It is fickle and violent: moments after hailing the assassins as honourable men, it rushes to tear apart the poet Cinna for no reason but his name. The people embody the theme of mob rule and the power of rhetoric: they are the prize the orators fight for, and the play shows how easily their love is won and how dangerously it is used.

entries.prompt: Loyalty and friendship
entries.answer: The excerpt values loyalty and friendship, and shows the cost of their betrayal. Caesar's death is a betrayal of trust — the stab of Brutus wounds him more than any other: "Et tu, Brute?" — while Antony's loyalty to his dead friend is honoured in the play: he risks his life to speak for Caesar and to hunt down his murderers. The value lesson: friendship is a bond that politics should not break; and the friend who betrays a friend, however noble the excuse, breaks something in himself that can never be mended.

entries.prompt: The responsibility of the public speaker
entries.answer: The scene teaches the weight of words. Brutus speaks for liberty and honesty; Antony speaks for revenge — and both move the same crowd. The value lesson is that rhetoric is a responsibility: the crowd that loves you today will act on your words tomorrow, and the orator who inflames a mob must answer for its deeds — from the murder of Cinna to the civil war. Words, the play warns, are like daggers: they kill; and the tongue that uses them carelessly, or cruelly, must carry the blame.

entries.prompt: Who wrote "Julius Caesar"?
entries.answer: William Shakespeare.

entries.prompt: What did Calpurnia dream?
entries.answer: That a statue of Caesar, spouting blood, was bathed in the washing of a hundred Romans.

entries.prompt: Name the omens Calpurnia reported.
entries.answer: A lioness whelping in the Capitol, the dead rising from their graves, men on fire but not burned, and warriors fighting in the clouds.

entries.prompt: How did Decius reinterpret Calpurnia's dream?
entries.answer: He said the blood was the people's love bathing in Caesar's blood, a sign that the Romans would receive life from him — a good omen.

entries.prompt: What did Metellus Cimber beg of Caesar?
entries.answer: That the banishment of his brother Publius Cimber be reversed.

entries.prompt: Where did Caesar fall?
entries.answer: At the foot of Pompey's statue, wrapped in his robe, stabbed by the conspirators.

entries.prompt: What were Caesar's last words?
entries.answer: "Et tu, Brute?" — "You too, Brutus?" — upon seeing Brutus among the assassins.

entries.prompt: Why did Brutus say he killed Caesar?
entries.answer: Not because he loved Caesar less, but because he loved Rome more — he feared Caesar's ambition would enslave the people.

entries.prompt: What did Caesar's will leave to every Roman citizen?
entries.answer: Seventy-five drachmas each, and his walks, gardens and orchards for all the people to enjoy.

entries.prompt: What happened to the poet Cinna?
entries.answer: The mob tore him to pieces because he bore the name of one of the conspirators.

entries.prompt: Compare Brutus's and Antony's speeches at the Forum.
entries.answer: Brutus speaks first, in plain and honest prose, asking the crowd to judge him as they judge him. He argues that he loved Caesar but loved Rome more — that Caesar's ambition would have enslaved them, and that he slew his best friend for the good of the commonwealth, offering his own dagger if ever Rome should need his death. The speech is reasoned, dignified and true to his character; it wins the crowd at once, and Brutus leaves, satisfied, trusting his honesty to speak for itself. Antony speaks second, and his art is in his irony. He opens by calling them "Friends, Romans, countrymen", claiming he comes to bury Caesar, not to praise him; and then, while repeating that the conspirators are "honourable men", he proves them false — Caesar wept with the poor, refused the crown three times, and enriched the people. He shows the bloody robe, weeps, pauses, and at last reads the will, which leaves seventy-five drachmas and the gardens to every Roman. Where Brutus appeals to reason, Antony appeals to pity, memory and self-interest; and in a single speech the crowd is turned from "honourable men" to a murderous mob.

entries.prompt: How does the crowd's mood change during Antony's oration?
entries.answer: At first the crowd is hostile to Antony — "He had no hand in his death" — and disposed to the conspirators. Antony plays them patiently. He begins modestly, insisting he has not come to praise Caesar; he builds sympathy by remembering Caesar's kindnesses; and with each repetition of "Brutus is an honourable man", his irony works deeper, planting doubt. When he shows Caesar's mantle, stabbed and bloody, the crowd murmurs; when he reveals the body and weeps, their pity turns to anger; and when he reads the will — seventy-five drachmas to every citizen, the walks and orchards for their pleasure — their anger becomes fury. They cry that Caesar was a tyrant no more; they resolve to burn the traitors' houses; and the crowd, which minutes before had hailed Brutus as honourable, now hunts his name through the streets and tears the innocent poet Cinna to pieces. The oration is a masterpiece of rhetoric — and a portrait of the fickleness of mobs, who love and hate at the word of a speaker.

entries.prompt: Why does Caesar fall at the foot of Pompey's statue, and why is this significant?
entries.answer: Caesar falls at the base of the statue of Pompey, the great general he defeated at Pharsalus — the man whose death had opened Caesar's road to absolute power. The staging is Shakespeare's irony: the tyrant falls at the monument of the man he destroyed, as if the old republic were claiming its revenge. Symbolically, the assassination is meant to restore the liberty of the old Rome that Pompey represented, yet the scene at the statue shows that the conspirators are repeating history, not mending it — killing a great man at the foot of a great man's image, in the very theatre of power. The blood of Caesar, spilling where Pompey's memory stands, announces that the republic will not be restored by daggers: the civil war that follows will drown the ideals of both Pompey and the conspirators, and Caesar's own heir will inherit the empire.

entries.prompt: Value question: What does the scene teach us about trust and betrayal?
entries.answer: The scene is a lesson in trust and its betrayal. Caesar trusts the Senate, the conspirators, and above all Brutus — the man he loves; and it is precisely that trust that undoes him. He is lured to the Capitol by flattery dressed as friendship; he is stabbed by men who embrace him; and his last words — "Et tu, Brute?" — are a cry of betrayal, not of pain: the deepest wound is not in his body but in the discovery that Brutus has a dagger. The lesson cuts both ways. Trust is noble: Antony, loyal to Caesar, survives the conspirators' city by his wits and avenges his friend. Betrayal is contagious: once the noblest man in Rome has joined the murder, no one is safe — the mob turns on the poet Cinna, and the conspiracy itself begins to tear itself apart. The value of the scene is that loyalty must be chosen carefully, honoured truly, and never betrayed for a phrase like "the good of Rome" — for words, as the play shows, can justify any dagger.

entries.prompt: How does Shakespeare use the theme of fate and omens in this excerpt?
entries.answer: Shakespeare thickens the scene with omens. Calpurnia's dream of the statue spouting blood; the lioness whelping in the Capitol; the dead rising from their graves; men walking with hands on fire yet unburned; warriors fighting in the clouds over the Capitol — all point to Caesar's death. The characters read them differently: Calpurnia reads them as fate's warning and begs Caesar to stay; Decius reinterprets the dream to feed Caesar's ambition; and Caesar, torn between superstition and pride, chooses the reading that flatters him. The irony is that the omens were true — the dream showed exactly what happened, a hundred Romans bathing in the blood of his statue — yet no reading could change the outcome, because the conspiracy was not made by fate but by men. Shakespeare's point is subtle: the portents are real, but they do not compel; they warn. Caesar's death comes not from the stars but from his own pride and the daggers of his friends — fate, in the end, is what men choose.

entries.prompt: Part 1 — The rival and the plan
entries.answer: Mrs Packletide longed to shoot a tiger — not out of love of hunting, but because Loona Bimberton, her rival, had recently been carried eleven miles in an aeroplane by an Algerian aviator. Only a personally procured tiger-skin and a heavy harvest of press photographs, Mrs Packletide felt, could counter that. She offered a thousand rupees to the villagers if they could arrange a tiger hunt in which she could shoot the tiger without much risk or exertion.

entries.prompt: Part 2 — The night of the shoot
entries.answer: The villagers found an old tiger that had taken to the village outskirts, and they tied up a goat as bait at the best distance for an easy shot. On a moonlit, cloudless night, Mrs Packletide and her paid companion Louisa Mebbin waited on a comfortable platform in a tree with an accurately sighted rifle. Miss Mebbin, ever mindful of money, complained the thousand rupees was too much for a public service. When the tiger came and the rifle flashed out, the beast sprang to one side and rolled over dead.

entries.prompt: Part 3 — The truth about the tiger
entries.answer: It was Louisa Mebbin who pointed out the embarrassing truth: the goat was in its death-throes from the bullet, while the tiger showed no wound at all. The old tiger had died of heart failure — frightened to death by the sudden report of the rifle, its shock accelerated by old age. The villagers, anxious for their thousand rupees, happily connived at the fiction that Mrs Packletide had shot the beast, and Miss Mebbin, being a paid companion, went along with it. Mrs Packletide's picture appeared in papers from the Texas Weekly Snapshot to the Novoe Vremya, and Loona Bimberton, green with envy, refused to look at illustrated papers for weeks.

entries.prompt: Part 4 — The blackmail and the lesson
entries.answer: A few days after a ball in honour of her triumph, Louisa Mebbin remarked that it would amuse everyone if they knew what had really happened — that Mrs Packletide had "shot the goat and frightened the tiger to death". When Mrs Packletide protested that no one would believe it, Miss Mebbin observed that Loona Bimberton would. The price of silence was a week-end cottage near Dorking, six hundred and eighty pounds freehold. Mrs Packletide paid, and Miss Mebbin's cottage, christened "Les Fauves" and gay with tiger-lilies, became the wonder of her friends. As for Mrs Packletide, she gave up big-game shooting for good: "The incidental expenses are so heavy," she confided.

entries.prompt: Vanity, jealousy and rivalry
entries.answer: The story's central theme is the absurdity of social rivalry. Mrs Packletide decides to shoot a tiger purely to outshine Loona Bimberton's aeroplane flight — a dangerous, expensive act undertaken out of vanity, not need. The whole enterprise is a hollow pretence: she does not even kill the tiger herself, yet claims the glory. The theme exposes how jealousy drives people to ridiculous lengths, and how the pursuit of status can cost far more than it is worth.

entries.prompt: Satire on upper-class pretension
entries.answer: Saki satirises the Edwardian upper classes, who treat a tiger hunt as a social occasion and a tiger-skin as a status symbol. The villagers connive for money, Miss Mebbin blackmails for a cottage, and the "heroine" accepts a glory she never earned. The satire is gentle but sharp: in a society obsessed with appearances, no one — from the sportswoman to the paid companion — is truly honest, and everyone is complicit in the great fiction of Mrs Packletide's tiger.

entries.prompt: Greed and exploitation
entries.answer: The theme of greed runs through the story. The villagers accept a thousand rupees to stage a fiction; Miss Mebbin, with her "protective elder-sister attitude towards money", turns her knowledge of the truth into a cottage worth six hundred and eighty pounds. Everyone in the story is willing to sell the truth for a price. The final irony is that Mrs Packletide's triumph leaves her poorer in every sense — she has paid far more, in blackmail and shame, than the tiger was ever worth.

entries.prompt: Mrs Packletide
entries.answer: Mrs Packletide is a rich Englishwoman driven by vanity and rivalry with Loona Bimberton. She wants the glory of killing a tiger without any of the danger, so she hires villagers to arrange a safe shot at an old, feeble tiger. She is proud, short-sighted and self-centred, yet she is also rather pathetic: her great triumph is a fraud, and she ends the story having paid dearly for a glory she never earned, giving up big-game shooting because "the incidental expenses are so heavy".

entries.prompt: Louisa Mebbin
entries.answer: Louisa Mebbin is Mrs Packletide's paid companion, and the story's real victor. She has a "morbid dread" of performing more service than she is paid for and a protective, almost elder-sisterly attitude towards money. She is the only one who notices the truth about the tiger's death, and she calmly turns that knowledge into blackmail: a week-end cottage near Dorking, which she christens "Les Fauves". Quiet, clever and mercenary, she outwits her employer completely while remaining perfectly pleasant.

entries.prompt: Loona Bimberton
entries.answer: Loona Bimberton is Mrs Packletide's social rival, the woman who had been carried eleven miles in an aeroplane by an Algerian aviator. She never appears directly in the action — we know her only by her effect on Mrs Packletide. After the tiger triumph she refuses to look at illustrated papers for weeks, and when forced to acknowledge the tiger-claw brooch Mrs Packletide sends her, she replies with a cold letter of thanks and declines the luncheon party. She represents the society Mrs Packletide is trying so hard to impress.

entries.prompt: The tiger
entries.answer: The tiger is the story's comic victim. It is an old, feeble animal that has been living in the jungle near the village, and the villagers consider it almost a public service to arrange its death. It ambles towards the tethered goat, springs aside at the rifle's report — and dies of heart failure, frightened to death by the noise, its demise accelerated by old age. It never receives a bullet, yet it becomes the centre of a great social triumph: proof that in this story, everything is pretence except the tiger's innocent death.

entries.prompt: Contentment is better than rivalry
entries.answer: The story teaches the folly of living for rivalry and show. Mrs Packletide spends a thousand rupees, stages a fraudulent hunt and ends up paying six hundred and eighty pounds in blackmail — all to outshine Loona Bimberton, who refuses to be impressed anyway. The value lesson: envy makes us pay heavily for what we do not truly need; contentment with one's own life is far cheaper and wiser than competing for the applause of others.

entries.prompt: Honesty costs less than pretence
entries.answer: The story shows that maintaining a lie is far more expensive than telling the truth. Mrs Packletide's tiny fraud — letting the world believe she shot the tiger — costs her a small fortune in blackmail and leaves her with a permanent fear of exposure. The lesson: pretence multiplies; every lie needs another lie and another payment to support it, while honesty, however humiliating in the moment, leaves nothing hanging over one's head.

entries.prompt: Why did Mrs Packletide want to shoot a tiger?
entries.answer: To outshine Loona Bimberton, who had recently been carried eleven miles in an aeroplane by an Algerian aviator.

entries.prompt: How much did Mrs Packletide offer the villagers?
entries.answer: A thousand rupees, to arrange a tiger hunt in which she could shoot the tiger without much risk.

entries.prompt: Who was Louisa Mebbin?
entries.answer: Mrs Packletide's paid companion, who was obsessed with money and performed only the service she was paid for.

entries.prompt: What was the bait for the tiger?
entries.answer: A goat, chosen because it bleated so persistently that even a partially deaf tiger might hear it on a still night.

entries.prompt: How did the tiger actually die?
entries.answer: It died of heart failure, frightened to death by the loud report of the rifle; the bullet had killed the goat, not the tiger.

entries.prompt: Why did the villagers support Mrs Packletide's story?
entries.answer: They were anxious for their thousand rupees and gladly connived at the fiction that she had shot the beast.

entries.prompt: What did Mrs Packletide send Loona Bimberton?
entries.answer: A tiger-claw brooch, which Loona acknowledged with a cold letter of thanks, refusing to attend the luncheon party.

entries.prompt: What was the price of Louisa Mebbin's silence?
entries.answer: A week-end cottage near Dorking, six hundred and eighty pounds freehold.

entries.prompt: What did Miss Mebbin name her cottage?
entries.answer: "Les Fauves" — French for "the wild beasts" — and its garden was gay with tiger-lilies in summer.

entries.prompt: Why did Mrs Packletide give up big-game shooting?
entries.answer: Because, as she confided, "the incidental expenses are so heavy".

entries.prompt: Describe the night of the tiger hunt. What really happened?
entries.answer: On a moonlit, cloudless night, Mrs Packletide and Louisa Mebbin took their places on a comfortable platform in a tree, with an accurately sighted rifle and a thumbnail pack of patience cards to pass the time. The villagers had tethered a persistently bleating goat at the best distance for an easy shot. Miss Mebbin, who had a morbid dread of doing more service than she was paid for, complained that the tiger was too old and a thousand rupees too much for what was, after all, a public service. When the tiger at last ambled towards the goat, the rifle flashed out with a loud report. The great tawny beast sprang to one side and then rolled over — dead. The villagers swarmed to the scene, rejoicing and beating tom-toms. But Louisa Mebbin drew attention to the awkward truth: the goat was in its death-throes from a mortal bullet-wound, while no trace of the rifle's work could be found on the tiger. The old tiger had died of heart failure, caused by the sudden report and accelerated by senile decay. The villagers, anxious for their thousand rupees, agreed to keep the secret, and Mrs Packletide faced the cameras with a light heart.

entries.prompt: How did Louisa Mebbin blackmail Mrs Packletide?
entries.answer: A few days after the ball Mrs Packletide gave in honour of her tiger triumph, Louisa Mebbin observed that "how amused every one would be if they knew what really happened". Asked what she meant, she reminded Mrs Packletide of the truth — that she had shot the goat and frightened the tiger to death. Mrs Packletide protested that no one would believe it, but Miss Mebbin calmly noted that Loona Bimberton would. Mrs Packletide's face settled on an unbecoming shade of greenish white as she asked, "You surely wouldn't give me away?" Miss Mebbin, with seeming irrelevance, remarked that she had seen a week-end cottage near Dorking she would like to buy — six hundred and eighty pounds, freehold — only she happened not to have the money. The bargain was struck, and in time Miss Mebbin's pretty cottage, christened "Les Fauves" and gay with tiger-lilies, became the wonder and admiration of her friends, who marvelled at how she managed it. Mrs Packletide never shot again.

entries.prompt: Value question: What does the story teach us about vanity and jealousy?
entries.answer: The story is a fable about the cost of vanity. Mrs Packletide does not need a tiger-skin; she needs to be seen to have one, because Loona Bimberton has had a moment of glory in an aeroplane. Jealousy persuades her to spend a thousand rupees, to accept a fake triumph, and then to pay six hundred and eighty pounds of blackmail to keep the fraud secret. In the end she has less than she began with: her purse is lighter, her honour is mortgaged to her paid companion, and her "triumph" is hollow. The lesson is that jealousy makes us pay for things we do not need, that rivals are seldom as impressed as we fear, and that the person who lives for the approval of others will never be satisfied. Contentment, the story suggests, is the only real economy.

entries.prompt: How does Saki use irony and satire in the story?
entries.answer: Saki builds the story on dramatic irony: the reader knows the tiger died of fright while the world believes Mrs Packletide shot it. Every part of the "triumph" is false — the shot missed, the glory is unearned, the photographs are lies — and yet the fiction succeeds completely, because everyone involved has a price. The satire is aimed at Edwardian high society, which treats a dangerous hunt as a fashion accessory and measures people by their press photographs; at the villagers, who gladly sell the truth for a thousand rupees; and at Louisa Mebbin, the "paid companion" who quietly outbids everyone and ends up the real victor. The final irony is delicious: Mrs Packletide, who risked everything to impress her rival, ends the story no longer hunting, with nothing to show but the heavy "incidental expenses" — while Miss Mebbin, the least glamorous person in the tale, walks away with the cottage of her dreams.

entries.prompt: Why can Louisa Mebbin be called the real winner of the story?
entries.answer: Louisa Mebbin wins because she understands the game everyone else is playing without knowing it. Mrs Packletide hunts for glory; Loona Bimberton glories in her flight; the villagers hunt for money. Miss Mebbin, by contrast, hunts for nothing but a fair price — she is the story's only practical person, with a "protective elder-sister attitude towards money". She notices what nobody else does (that the tiger has no bullet wound), she assesses the value of her silence correctly (a cottage, six hundred and eighty pounds), and she conducts her blackmail so pleasantly that her friends can only wonder "how Louisa manages to do it". In a story where everyone trades the truth for something, she trades it for the best price and keeps her hands clean. The others end poorer or humiliated; Miss Mebbin ends with a beautiful cottage — proof that in this society, the person who understands money best walks away with everything.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Stanza 1 — The boast of immortality
entries.answer: The poem opens with the poet's great boast: neither marble nor the gilded monuments of princes shall outlive his powerful rhyme. He tells the loved one that she shall shine more bright in this poem than in unswept stone besmeared with sluttish time — that is, than in neglected statues and tombs that time soils and defaces. Where the proud monuments of rulers are destroyed by wasteful war and ruined by the ravages of time, the words of his verse will live on, refusing to be worn away.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Stanza 2 — The war against time and war
entries.answer: The second movement of the poem strengthens the boast. The poet declares that neither Mars, the god of war, nor his sword, nor the quick flames of burning war, nor all the accidents of time — no war, no ruin, no destruction — can erase the living record of his love. The loved one's memory shall outlive all the monuments that hate and strife have levelled, and her name will be carried forward as long as there are eyes to read and men to remember. Where princes' statues fall, the poem stands.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Stanza 3 — The judgment to come
entries.answer: The boast reaches its height in the final vision. The poet declares that his loved one shall live on in the poem until the day of judgment — "the ending doom" — when the last trumpet calls the dead to rise and all the world is judged. Even then, she shall be present in his verse, alive and remembered, whereas those who depend on stone will have vanished into the dust of time. The poem's final lines promise that her memory will stand so long as men can breathe and eyes can see — and that this verse, and the love it records, will live and give life to her.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Poetry outlives stone
entries.answer: The central theme of the poem is the victory of art over time. Marble, gold and the proud monuments of princes are all perishable: they are defaced by weather, broken by war, and forgotten with their builders. But the poet's verse — "this powerful rhyme" — survives all that. The theme is an act of faith in language: the written word, the poet claims, can outlive stone, can carry a name and a love across centuries, and can raise the loved one brighter than any statue. For Shakespeare, the truest monument is not built of marble but of rhyme.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: The immortality of love
entries.answer: The poem is also a love poem, and its promise is the immortality of love. The poet writes to give his loved one eternal life: she shall shine in his verse, live in his lines, and be remembered "so long as men can breathe or eyes can see". The love recorded here is not subject to time's decay — war cannot destroy it, ruin cannot erase it, and even the last judgment will find her alive in the poem. The theme unites love and art: it is the poet's love that powers the verse, and the verse that makes the love eternal.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: The vanity of worldly monuments
entries.answer: Against the poem stands the vanity of worldly glory. The monuments of princes — marble, gilded tombs — are built to defy time and are defeated by it: unswept stone is besmeared with sluttish time, wars waste the proudest buildings, and ruin levels what hate and strife have built. The theme is a lesson in humility: power, wealth and pride leave behind nothing that time will not wear away. What the great build for themselves decays; what the poet writes for love endures. True immortality, the poem suggests, belongs to art and love, not to stone and gold.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Personification of time
entries.answer: Time is personified throughout the poem. It is "sluttish time" — careless, filthy, neglectful — which besmears the unswept stone of monuments; it is a destroyer that levels buildings and wrecks the work of princes. Time is pictured as an enemy against which the poet fights with his rhyme, and as a wearer-down of all that men build. The personification gives the abstract force of time a face and a character: careless in its neglect, ruthless in its ruin. Against this personified tyrant, only the poem can stand.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: The sonnet form
entries.answer: The poem is a sonnet — fourteen lines of iambic pentameter with the rhyme scheme abab cdcd efef gg. The three quatrains each advance the boast: the first contrasts the poem with stone, the second with war, and the third with the day of judgment. The final couplet — "So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee" — is the poem's climax and its promise, neatly rhyming to seal the argument. The sonnet's strict form is itself the theme in miniature: the most disciplined of forms, carrying the most defiant of boasts, that form itself will outlast the world.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Contrast and antithesis
entries.answer: The poem's argument is built on contrasts: marble against rhyme, gilded monuments against living words, the prince's tomb against the loved one's memory, the ruin of war against the lasting of verse. The antitheses work on both sides of the boast: what is mighty — stone, gold, power, war — is shown to be perishable; what is humble — a poem — is shown to be eternal. The contrast sharpens with each quatrain, until the final couplet opposes the last thing of all: the ending of the world against the life of the poem. The structure of the contrasts is the poem's engine, driving home its single boast.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Hyperbole
entries.answer: The poem's boast is delivered in hyperbole — deliberate, magnificent exaggeration. The poet claims his rhyme shall outlive marble, gilded monuments, wasteful war, the god of war's own sword, fire, ruin, and time itself; that the loved one shall live until the ending doom; that her memory shall outwalk the levelled monuments of princes. Each claim is more extravagant than the last, rising to the final promise: so long as men breathe, the verse lives. The hyperbole is not empty: it is the argument of the poem in its boldest form — the poet stakes everything on the power of the word, and the exaggeration is the measure of his faith. A modest claim, the poem suggests, would be a modest love; the grandeur of the boast matches the grandeur of the feeling it protects.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: The imagery of stone and ruin
entries.answer: The poem's imagery is dominated by stone and ruin. We see "marble" and "gilded monuments", "unswept stone besmeared" with time's neglect, monuments wasted by "wars", buildings levelled by "ruin", and the work of "Mars" destroyed by fire and battle. The imagery is deliberately heavy, solid, grand — and it is all doomed. Against this weight of stone stands the lightness of the "rhyme" and the "living record" of memory. The contrast of images is the poem's picture-language: the heavier the stone, the stronger the boast that words will outlast it.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Why does the poet choose the "powerful rhyme" as the true monument?
entries.answer: The poet chooses rhyme because he has seen what happens to stone. Marble and gilded monuments are at the mercy of time and war: they are defaced, broken, levelled, and at last forgotten. A poem, by contrast, lives in the mind and on the tongue; it is carried by readers, repeated, remembered; it needs no foundation and fears no fire. The "powerful rhyme" is powerful precisely because it is small: it slips through the disasters that destroy statues, surviving by being read. Shakespeare's boast is also a theory of art: the written word is the most durable human thing because it can be endlessly re-born in new readers — "so long as men can breathe or eyes can see". The poem argues that the monument of language outlasts the monument of stone because it is not a thing but a life.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: How does the poem treat war and destruction?
entries.answer: War is pictured as the great wrecker of monuments. The poem names "wasteful war" and "Mars his sword" and the "quick flames" of burning war as the forces that undo what princes build — and then dismisses them all in a single stroke: none of them shall "outlive this powerful rhyme". The treatment is remarkable for its calm: the poet does not rage against war but simply declares its limits. War can break stone, raze buildings, level the proudest tombs; it cannot erase a line of verse, because verse does not live in stone but in minds. The poem's calm confidence — that even the god of war is beaten by a rhyme — is the height of its boast, and the deepest expression of its faith in the power of words over the power of arms.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: The worth of art over wealth
entries.answer: The poem teaches us to value the enduring over the impressive. Marble and gold are impressive, but they perish; a poem, a song, a word of love endures. The value lesson is about where we build our monuments: the princes build in stone and are forgotten, while the poet builds in rhyme and gives life. For students of the poem, the lesson is to invest in the things that outlast us — in art, in writing, in love, in memory — rather than in the glitter of things that time will soil. The poem's boast is a quiet sermon on the worth of the spirit over the show.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: The power of remembrance
entries.answer: The poem is also a lesson in remembrance. The poet undertakes to remember the loved one forever — to carry her memory through war, time and judgment — and his verse becomes the vessel of that promise. The value lesson: remembrance is an act of love, and the truest way to honour someone is to remember them — in words, in stories, in the living practice of those who come after. The poem promises that so long as the poem is read, the loved one lives. It teaches us that what we remember of people is more lasting than any statue we build to them.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Who wrote "Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments"?
entries.answer: William Shakespeare — it is Sonnet 55.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: What shall outlive the marble and gilded monuments?
entries.answer: The poet's powerful rhyme — his verse.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: How is time personified in the poem?
entries.answer: As "sluttish time", which soils and defaces the unswept stone of monuments.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Name the forces the poem says cannot destroy the verse.
entries.answer: Wasteful war, Mars's sword, the quick flames of burning war, and the ravages of time.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: What form is the poem written in?
entries.answer: A Shakespearean sonnet — fourteen lines with the rhyme scheme abab cdcd efef gg.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Until when shall the loved one live in the poem?
entries.answer: Until "the ending doom" — the day of judgment, when the dead rise.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: What is the promise of the final couplet?
entries.answer: So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, this poem lives — and gives life to the loved one.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: What does the poem say happens to the monuments of princes?
entries.answer: They are wasted by war, levelled by ruin, and besmeared and forgotten by time.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: What is the central theme of the poem?
entries.answer: That poetry and love outlive marble, gold, war and time itself.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Against whom is the boast of the poem directed?
entries.answer: Against time and destruction — war, ruin, and the decay that destroys worldly monuments.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Explain the argument of the poem, stanza by stanza.
entries.answer: The sonnet argues its boast in three waves, capped by a couplet. In the first quatrain the poet sets up the contrast: marble and the gilded monuments of princes shall not outlive his powerful rhyme; the loved one shall shine brighter in his verse than in unswept stone besmeared with sluttish time — for the finest statue decays, while the poem does not. In the second quatrain he strengthens the claim against the violent forces: not wasteful war, not Mars's sword, not the quick flames of burning conflict, not the ruin that levels the proudest buildings — none can erase the "living record" of his love; her memory shall outwalk the monuments that hatred and strife destroy. In the third quatrain he carries the boast to the farthest horizon: the loved one shall live in the poem until the ending doom, the last judgment when all the dead rise; even then she shall be found alive in his lines, while the stone monuments stand forgotten. The couplet seals the promise in the most famous lines of the poem: so long as men breathe and eyes see, this verse lives — and gives life to her. The whole poem is one continuous ascent: from the grave of stone, through the fires of war, to the gates of judgment, the rhyme alone ascends.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: What is the poem's attitude towards time and worldly glory?
entries.answer: The poem regards time as a slovenly destroyer and worldly glory as vanity. Time is not pictured as noble or just but as "sluttish" — careless, filthy, neglecting what it should preserve; it besmears the unswept stone of monuments and levels the work of princes. Worldly glory — the marble, the gilding, the pride of rulers — is shown to be hollow: it is wasted by war, burnt by fire, ruined by ruin, and at last forgotten. The poet's attitude is thus a kind of contempt: the grandest tomb is only "unswept stone" in time's careless house, and the proudest prince builds a monument for the worm. Against this, the poem sets the humblest of things — a rhyme, a record, a memory — and declares it imperishable. The attitude is at once satirical towards power and confident in art: glory built on stone is vanity, but glory built on words is life. The poem's quiet lesson is that the world's monuments are dust, and the world's writers are its true immortals.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Value question: What does the poem teach us about the things that truly last?
entries.answer: The poem is a lesson in what is lasting. Marble, gold, palaces, the tombs of princes — all the things we build to be remembered — the poem declares perishable: time soils them, war wastes them, ruin levels them. What lasts is not things but words and love: the verse that records a name, the memory that carries a person forward, the love that keeps a life alive in the minds of readers. The value lesson for us is to spend ourselves on what endures — on art, on writing, on kindness, on the care we give to people — rather than on monuments of stone and show. The poem's boast is also its sermon: build your memorial in living things, in poems and memories and love, and no war, no time, no judgment can take it from you. What we give to people, the poem says, outlasts what we build for ourselves.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: How does the final couplet complete the poem's argument?
entries.answer: The final couplet — "So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee" — is the poem's climax and its foundation. The three quatrains have argued that rhyme outlasts stone, that verse survives war, that memory endures to the last judgment; the couplet now rests the whole boast on the smallest and simplest condition: as long as humanity continues — men breathe, eyes see, readers read — the poem lives. And because the poem lives, the loved one lives: the verse is not merely a monument to her but a means of life, a vessel in which she is reborn every time it is read. The couplet is both the poem's proof and its promise: the argument closes in a circle of life — the poem lives in readers, the loved one lives in the poem. It is the most compressed statement in English of art's great claim: that what is written with love outlasts the world that wrote it.

entries.unitTitle: Not Marble nor the Gilded Monuments
entries.prompt: Why is the poem called a love poem as well as a boast about poetry?
entries.answer: The poem is a boast about poetry, but the boast is made in the service of love. The poet does not write to praise his own skill but to immortalise the loved one: her memory, her name, her life are what the verse is sworn to protect. The poem's energies — the defiance of time, the defiance of war, the vision of the last judgment — are all directed to one end: that she shall not be forgotten. Poetry is the instrument; love is the purpose. The boast is also the promise: because the poet loves her, he will not let time take her; he will build her a monument of words that outlasts every stone. The theme of the poem is thus double: art is powerful, and love is the power of art. The sonnet is a love poem because it gives the loved one life — and it gives her life because it is a poem, and it is a poem because it loves her.

entries.prompt: Part 1 — The traveller's tale
entries.answer: The poet meets a traveller from an antique land, who tells him of a desert where two vast and trunkless legs of stone stand in the sand, and beside them lies a shattered visage — half sunk in the sand, its frown, wrinkled lip and sneer of cold command still readable on the broken face. The sculptor who carved the face understood the passions of the king who commanded it, and stamped them on the stone, so that even in ruin the face speaks: the hand that mocked them and the heart that fed them are gone, but the passions remain, read by the passer-by.

entries.prompt: Part 2 — The words on the pedestal
entries.answer: On the pedestal of the shattered statue, the traveller reads these words: "My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings: Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!" The boast is colossal: the king commands all future powers to look on his works and lose hope of matching them. But around the statue, the traveller says, there is nothing — nothing but the lone and level sands stretching far away. The ruin of the desert is the answer to the boast: the king's works are gone, his name survives only on a broken stone, and the Mighty who look on this are taught, not despair, but humility.

entries.prompt: The vanity of power and pride
entries.answer: The poem's central theme is the vanity of human power. Ozymandias called himself "King of Kings" and commanded all who saw his works to despair — yet nothing of his works remains but two stone legs and a shattered face in an empty desert. The boast is answered by the desert: the tyrant's pride is swallowed by the sands, and his name lives only as a lesson in ruin. The theme teaches that power is transient, pride is hollow, and the mightiest of kings becomes, in time, the dust that blows across his own kingdom.

entries.prompt: Time's triumph over all things
entries.answer: The poem is a meditation on time, the great leveler. Time breaks the statue's legs, buries its face, erases the kingdom, and turns the "works" of the king into the lone and level sands. The artist's skill, too, is defeated in the end: the sculptor's masterpiece is half sunk in the sand, and the passions stamped on the stone will themselves crumble. Only the boast — and the irony of it — survives, and even that survives only because time has made it true in reverse. The theme: nothing man builds outlasts time; the desert is time's monument.

entries.prompt: Art versus the artist's subject
entries.answer: The poem sets the artist against the tyrant. Ozymandias commanded a sculptor to immortalise him; the sculptor did his work so well that the "passions" of the king — the frown, the sneer of cold command — survive in stone long after the king is dust. But the irony is complete: the art outlives the king only to expose him. The sneer that mocked the sculptor's hand is now mocked by the desert; the heart that fed on the passions of cruelty has fed the sands. Art, the poem suggests, is more lasting than power — but even art is dust in the face of time, and the truest monument is the poem itself, which teaches the lesson.

entries.prompt: Irony
entries.answer: The poem is built on one colossal irony. The pedestal's boast — "Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!" — is spoken in a desert where there are no works at all; the traveller's eye, looking around, finds nothing but the lone and level sands. The "King of Kings" is a king of nothing; the command to despair falls on the empty air. The irony is doubled by the poem's survival: the boast is remembered only because it is so perfectly disproved. The shattered face and the grand words together make the poem's point: the louder the boast, the louder the fall.

entries.prompt: The frame narrative
entries.answer: The poem uses a frame narrative: the poet speaks first, then reports the words of a traveller "from an antique land", who in turn reports the words written on the pedestal. The device creates distance — the king's boast is relayed through two voices and an unknown span of time, as if the poem were an archaeological find. The frame also builds the poem's irony: we hear the boast second-hand, from the ruins, and we can see what the king could not — the empty desert around the shattered stone. The layered voices make the poem a kind of testimony: the traveller testifies to the ruin, and the poet testifies to the lesson.

entries.prompt: The sonnet form
entries.answer: The poem is a sonnet — fourteen lines — but Shelley bends the form to his subject. The octave (the first eight lines) sets the scene: the traveller's tale of the legs, the shattered face, the sculptor's art. The sestet (the last six) delivers the boast and its ironic answer: the words on the pedestal, and then the lone and level sands. The volta, or turn, comes at the moment the pedestal is read — the boast — and the poem turns it inside out with the desert. The tight, disciplined form holds the wild emptiness of the desert in tension, giving the poem its power.

entries.prompt: Imagery of ruin and emptiness
entries.answer: The poem's imagery is spare and desolate: two vast and trunkless legs of stone, a shattered visage half sunk in the sand, a pedestal in a desert, and the lone and level sands stretching far away. Every image is a negation — legs without a trunk, a face without a body, a monument without a kingdom, a king without works. The "sneer of cold command" is the one vivid, living image, and even it survives only on broken stone. The imagery teaches the poem's lesson without a word of moralising: the reader sees the ruin and knows the boast is empty.

entries.prompt: Alliteration and sound
entries.answer: Shelley's sound-work deepens the poem's mood. The "s" sounds of "sands", "sunk", "sneer", "stamped", "sculptor", "stretch" and "shattered" whisper through the poem like wind across the desert — the poem itself sounds like the bare level sand. The alliteration binds the images: the "cold command", the "sneer of cold command", the "lone and level sands" whose repeated "l" sounds stretch the line out, as if the desert were visible in the sound. The poem's music is minimal and dry — appropriate to a landscape of dust — and its emptiness is felt in the ear as well as the eye.

entries.prompt: Why does the poem end with the image of the lone and level sands?
entries.answer: The final image is the poem's verdict. The pedestal boasts of works; the poem answers with emptiness — "Nothing beside remains" — and then expands that nothing into the only visible thing: the lone and level sands stretching far away. The sands are the true "works" of the desert: level, endless, featureless, the negation of every monument. The image does three things at once. It confirms the irony, showing the king's boast answered by vacancy. It gives time a face, picturing the ages that have smoothed every trace of the kingdom. And it closes the poem in stillness and scale — the reader is left standing in the same desert, looking on the same nothing, and the boast of the "King of Kings" shrinks to a whisper on the wind.

entries.prompt: What is the role of the sculptor in the poem?
entries.answer: The sculptor is the poem's quiet hero — and its quiet victim. He was commanded by the tyrant to immortalise him, and he did his work with terrible fidelity: he "read" the passions of the king — the frown, the wrinkled lip, the sneer of cold command — and stamped them into the stone, so that the face survives the hand that mocked it and the heart that fed it. The sculptor outlives the king in his work; yet the poem's irony touches him too, for the art that preserves the king also preserves his cruelty, and the work that was built to defy time is half sunk in the sand. The sculptor is the poem's proof that art is stronger than power — and time is stronger than art.

entries.prompt: How does the poem's form match its theme?
entries.answer: The sonnet's strict form — fourteen lines, tightly turned — is the perfect vessel for a poem about ruin. The discipline of the form stands against the wildness of the desert, as the poem's civilisation stands against the waste it describes. The octave is all scene and craft: the traveller, the legs, the face, the sculptor's art — a carefully built picture. The sestet is all collapse: the boast, and then the nothing. The volta, the turn, lands exactly where the pedestal is read, and the poem turns from the king's voice to the desert's silence. The form does what the sculptor does: it stamps meaning on the void. And like the statue, the poem's very orderliness is what makes the emptiness felt — the neatest sonnet describing the emptiest landscape in English poetry.

entries.prompt: Pride comes before the fall
entries.answer: The poem is the oldest of lessons told anew: pride goes before destruction. Ozymandias called himself King of Kings and believed his works would make the mighty despair; time answered with a desert. The value lesson is humility — the knowledge that power, wealth and fame are lent to us, not owned, and that the boast built on them will be read, in the end, by the wind. The poem does not preach; it shows. The king's sneer is stamped on stone, and the stone is sunk in sand. He who exalts himself, the poem says, will be levelled; and the only true monument is the lesson, remembered.

entries.prompt: The lasting worth of the artist
entries.answer: Against the king stands the sculptor — and the poet. The king's works are dust, but the sculptor's reading of him survives, and the poem that remembers the whole scene survives in the reader's mind. The value lesson: creation outlasts conquest. The tyrant builds with fear; the artist builds with understanding — and understanding outlives fear. The poem honours the quiet craft of the sculptor and the poet over the loud command of the king: what is made with care and truth remains, when what is made with force and pride has crumbled to the lone and level sands.

entries.prompt: Who wrote "Ozymandias"?
entries.answer: P.B. Shelley, the Romantic poet.

entries.prompt: Who tells the poet about the statue?
entries.answer: A traveller from an antique land.

entries.prompt: What remains of the statue in the desert?
entries.answer: Two vast and trunkless legs of stone, and beside them a shattered visage half sunk in the sand.

entries.prompt: What is written on the pedestal?
entries.answer: "My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings: Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!"

entries.prompt: What does the traveller see around the statue?
entries.answer: Nothing — only the lone and level sands stretching far away.

entries.prompt: What did the sculptor read and stamp on the stone?
entries.answer: The passions of the king — his frown, wrinkled lip and sneer of cold command.

entries.prompt: What form is the poem written in?
entries.answer: A sonnet of fourteen lines, with an octave and a sestet.

entries.prompt: What is the central theme of the poem?
entries.answer: The vanity of power and pride — time destroys all human works.

entries.prompt: What irony lies in the words on the pedestal?
entries.answer: The king commands the mighty to look on his works and despair — but there are no works left, only ruins and sand.

entries.prompt: What survives longer than the king's works in the poem?
entries.answer: The sculptor's art (the carved passions) and the poet's verse that remembers it.

entries.prompt: Describe the scene the traveller reports.
entries.answer: The traveller describes a desert of colossal ruin. Two vast and trunkless legs of stone stand in the sand — the remains of a statue so large that its legs alone are enormous — but the body they once supported is gone. Beside them lies the shattered visage, the face of the statue, half sunk in the sand, so that only part of it is visible. Yet the face still speaks: its frown, its wrinkled lip and its "sneer of cold command" are clearly readable in the stone, and they tell us of the king who commanded the work — a tyrant whose passions were so strong that they were stamped into his own likeness. The traveller reflects that the sculptor who carved the face understood those passions perfectly and preserved them, so that the hand that mocked the king and the heart that fed on his cruelties are both gone, yet their record remains. On the pedestal stand the king's boastful words — and all around, nothing but the lone and level sands stretching far away. The scene is the poem's whole argument in pictures: a monument, a boast, and a desert.

entries.prompt: Explain the irony of the words on the pedestal.
entries.answer: The words on the pedestal are the boast of a tyrant at the height of his power: "My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings: Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!" The king commands every future power to gaze on his achievements and despair of ever equalling them. The irony is absolute, because the traveller reports the boast from a desert where nothing of the king's works remains: the statue is shattered, its body gone, its face sunk in the sand, and the kingdom itself has vanished — "Nothing beside remains". The Mighty who read the words today are taught, not despair at the king's greatness, but humility at his ruin. The boast has survived only in its own destruction: the words are remembered precisely because they are so completely disproved. The king who called himself King of Kings is now the king of a heap of stone in an empty desert — and the only despair the monument inspires is the despair of pride itself.

entries.prompt: Value question: What does the poem teach us about power and pride?
entries.answer: The poem teaches the oldest of lessons: power is borrowed, and pride is perishable. Ozymandias possessed an empire and commanded a monument to outlast it; time reduced both to rubble and sand. The value lesson is humility — not the humility of self-deprecation, but the knowledge that every boast is spoken over a grave. The poem shows that what we build with force and fear is blown away, while what is made with understanding — the sculptor's craft, the poet's verse, the truth of a lesson — endures. It teaches us to weigh our lives by lasting things: kindness, craft, truth, memory — not by the sneer of cold command. And it teaches us to read history honestly: the mighty of every age believe their works are eternal; the next age finds their name on a broken stone in a desert. The poem's quiet command to us is to build what time cannot despise.

entries.prompt: What is the poet's attitude towards the king?
entries.answer: The poet's attitude is one of calm, ironic judgment — no rage, no triumph, simply the picture and the desert.
